blogs.name: Simon Willison's Weblog
blogs.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
blogs.description: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden…
blogs.content:
Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!

 Weight-Space Programming

 Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:

 Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

 Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

 All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming .

 The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.

 spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.

 I'm going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.

 The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games - Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it's an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question:

 The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response.

 The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games:

 breakout/prompt.txt

 freeway/prompt.txt

 pacman/prompt.txt

 pong/prompt.txt

 I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others.

 Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models

 The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this:

 llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \
 -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro

 This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here's what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens.

 But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That's still my favorite model to run on my own laptop - it's just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025.

 I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command:

 LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \
 llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \
 -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b

 (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .)

 After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here's the reasoning trace ):

 Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets.

 Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards.

 Confidence: 72%

 This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong ( reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s:

 Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object.

 Description:

 The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized.

 Confidence:

 75%

 And Breakout ( reasoning ) in 52m 25s:

 Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game.

 Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty.

 Confidence: 88%

 Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn't surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here's that transcript - Qwen thought it was "A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally".

 The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here's a sample:

 What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let's list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right?

 That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort.

 It's a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I've seen around it does not feel justified. I'm not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways.

 Tags: machine-learning , ai , generative-ai , local-llms , llms , qwen , paper-review

I discovered a sound that leaks your exact location (and it's everywhere) - YouTube

Genius piece of OSINT by Colsto, who demonstrates how you can take almost imperceptible background noise of planes from a video soundtrack, figure out their Doppler curves, then cross reference them against ADS-B data to find the exact location of the video based on their speed, distance, and gaps between different flights.

 Via Lobste.rs

blogs.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 4,563 new readers. Every few weeks, it seems another leading AI lab says that an autonomous AI researcher is closer to reality. New MIT research just gave a peek at how much of that capability may be sitting inside models already available to the public.
 GPT-6 Astra went inside a smaller AI with poor math scores and improved it directly, skipping the training that normally does that work. Once improving a model is as simple as pointing another one at it, AI’s already frantic pace could hit another gear.

---
 In today’s AI rundown:
 OpenAI’s Astra rewrites other AI from the inside

 OpenAI grades its AI on everyday tasks

 Turn one interview into two clips with Riverside

 OpenAI joins Abu Dhabi’s AI-native government push

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 AI RESEARCH
 🔬  OpenAI’s Astra rewrites other AI from the inside
 Image source: MIT CSAIL

 The Rundown: MIT researchers just published research showing that OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra can improve some AI models by directly rewriting their weights — the numbers that decide how a model behaves — rather than putting them through more training.
 The details:
 Weights are normally set through training, since even small AI models have far too many to read or adjust by hand.

 Alibaba’s small Qwen model scored 7.9% in math until Astra changed just 0.016% of those weights to cut its habit of repeating itself, hitting 48.1% after the fix.

 The same approach did little for Google’s smaller Gemma 3, which lacked a single flaw like Qwen’s repetition, barely moving its math score.

 Smaller tests also had Astra name the game an AI had learned from its weights alone, and write a simple Breakout player from scratch without training.

 The authors say this capability could one day let AI upgrade itself, add or remove skills in other models on request, or check them for hidden problems.

 Why it matters: The top AI labs are racing toward self-improving, automated AI researchers, and while this research is just one small example, it may be a sign of where things are headed. Once models are strong enough to alter and improve their weights, we’re in major “takeoff” territory, where AI starts speeding up its own progress.

 TOGETHER WITH OPTIMIZELY
 🔎  Finding AI use cases in your workflows

 The Rundown: When it comes to AI planning, the highest-value use cases are already living inside your workflows — you just have to know where to look. Optimizely’s template helps you find AI use cases that really matter in just a few minutes.
 The template gives you:
 A 3-step framework to build the foundation of your next AI agent

 The exact process that turned a 2-3 hour GA4 reporting task into a 5-minute one

 Real use cases mapped to how your team actually works

 Download the template for better AI use cases .

 OPENAI
 📋 OpenAI grades its AI on everyday tasks
 Image source: OpenAI

 The Rundown: OpenAI just introduced LifeVal, a new test grading how well AI gets through everyday errands like booking appointments, buying groceries, and filling out government forms, with tasks chosen based on what people say they want help with.
 The details:
 The selected task areas come from a poll of 4K people on where they want help, and global time-use surveys on what everyday tasks consume time.

 LifeVal has been OpenAI’s internal measurement for the past year, as it trained models to browse the web, operate a computer, and work in connected apps.

 OpenAI’s models have gone from an average score of 49.3% (GPT-5.2) to 80.6% (GPT-6 Astra), though just 0.6 points of that gain came after July’s GPT-5.6.

 Astra’s “best recorded” scores hit 100% on 10 of 16 tasks OpenAI listed, like replacing a lost engagement ring, with LSAT help scoring the lowest at 88.7%.

 Why it matters: We look at benchmark results on everything from coding and math to business tasks, but few have measured how models handle the everyday tasks that a more general audience is asking AI to do. Seeing this eval tested across other models would be an interesting data point for the personal agent meta seen across the industry.

 AI TRAINING
 🎬  Turn one interview into two clips with Riverside

 The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll use Riverside’s new agents to turn a licensed interview into two captioned videos. You’ll choose useful moments, check the edits, and prepare post drafts without filming anything new.
 Step-by-step:
 Download the guide’s openly licensed interview and save its credit. Then, make an MP4 copy and upload it to a Riverside practice project

 Ask Clipper for short passages that make sense on their own. Make sure to watch the surrounding interview before choosing your two clips

 Ask Editor for a matching vertical layout, keeping the full picture visible and leaving space for captions and the source label

 Check the captions against the speech, then ask Marketer for two short post drafts. Keep the interview’s date and full credit with each one

 Finally, export both clips and watch the saved files. Check the framing, sound, words, and ending before handing them off

 Pro tip: A shorter clip can change what someone seems to mean. Keep the question or qualifying sentence when the answer depends on it. Visit The Rundown University to get the full guide, materials, files, and more.

 PRESENTED BY PAVE
 🔧  The simple fix for apps that stall

 The Rundown: Vibe coding makes building apps fast. But it’s also left piles of slick-looking apps that sit unused because they can’t talk to the tools you rely on every day. Pave gives you the speed without the dead end.
 With Pave, you can:
 Describe your process and get a working custom app in minutes

 Link to 350+ systems, including Quickbase, on every plan

 Create workflows to run reminders, approvals, and handoffs on their own

 Build now .

 AI & THE WORLD
 🤝  OpenAI joins Abu Dhabi’s AI-native government push
 Image source: Abu Dhabi Media Office

 The Rundown: OpenAI just sealed four agreements in Abu Dhabi, bringing its AI to state oil giant ADNOC, the emirate’s government, and state investor Mubadala, while a UAE group is reportedly set to be the top investor in the AI giant’s raise of up to $20B.
 The details:
 ADNOC’s deal, the largest of the four, aims to cut oil field planning from months to hours by running decades of well data through OpenAI’s models.

 Food imports come first in “Machine-Readable Government,” a project turning some Abu Dhabi rules into text AI can read to help streamline permit processes.

 Abu Dhabi already has a $3.5B plan for AI across all public services, and a separate OpenAI and Microsoft program aims to train 20K staff and the public.

 OpenAI’s models will help Mubadala weigh risk and spot new bets, while a five-year pact with AI firm G42’s Inception42 targets UAE businesses and schools.

 Why it matters: Albania gained headlines last year by naming a digital AI “minister,” but Abu Dhabi’s version is more practical — giving AI better access to existing data and rules to improve efficiency. The circular AI dealmaking also continues, with Abu Dhabi acting as both a major deployer of OpenAI’s tech and potentially the biggest investor.

 QUICK HITS

 COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY
 ▸ Judd built an AI research team that fact-checks itself
 Today’s workflow comes from reader Judd Slivka:
 “I use a four-step system built on Grok Bot to get AI-generated research reports with fewer errors. It’s for anyone who relies on AI research and needs to trust the numbers and quotes in it.
 I start with a research bot that has specific instructions. They cover the types of sources it should use, separating known facts from speculative claims, and cross-checking claims. The report goes to a skeptic. The skeptic is meant to be contrarian but not a roadblock. It asks for evidence, looks for logical fallacies, and creates a short, ranked list of problems. The problem list goes back to the researcher, who then passes the report to my fact-checker. The fact-checker double-checks every number and every quote or paraphrase against the actual document it was found in.
 The result is a report with fewer errors, but also flags on what’s verified and what isn’t. Far and away the most valuable workflow that I’ve built. It costs more in terms of usage, but it’s been working great.”
 See the workflow on our Community Workflow Hub →

blogs.name: Tomasz Tunguz
blogs.title: The Financial Engineering Essential for AI in 2027
blogs.description: The essential ingredient to AI has more than doubled in cost in the last 6 months. GPUs, the chips that power AI, have increased in rental…
blogs.content:
The essential ingredient to AI has more than doubled in cost in the last 6 months.

 GPUs, the chips that power AI, have increased in rental price per hour from $3 to $12 to $13 on short-term contracts, pushing Anthropic’s blended cost per GPU-equivalent hour from $3.10 to $5.65 (within a $3.45 to $8.29 confidence band), according to data from the updated Anthropic S-1/A 1 2 .

 Anthropic, like other AI providers, is trying to rent as many accelerators as possible on multi-year contracts that fix prices around $2 to $4 per hour. When that long-term capacity is exhausted, AI vendors must buy access to GPUs in the short-term burst market, where prices have surged 1 .

 This cost spike changes the unit economics of a frontier lab. A doubling of GPU cost must be met by a doubling of model efficiency, a doubling of price to the customer, or a combination of the two to preserve margins.

 With 40% to 50% of data center projects delayed 3 & billions of dollars of GPUs sitting idle in warehouses waiting for power 4 , plus transformer & turbine lead times measured in years 5 , this supply pressure shows no sign of easing in the near term.

 Meanwhile, the price war across frontier & mid-tier models 6 makes raising token prices perilous : any lab that hikes rates cedes share.

 Labs are responding on three fronts : engineering step-function gains in model efficiency like Opus 5.5’s 40% reduction in cost per task over Opus 5 1 , tightening subscription allowances like OpenAI’s move to pool ChatGPT & Codex into a single shared token limit 7 , & pushing enterprise buyers from serverless API consumption into multi-year committed contracts.

 Financial engineering in 2027 means closing that duration mismatch : selling a Fortune 500 buyer a multi-year minimum commitment at a locked-in rate to match the duration of the GPU lease underneath it.

 In 2026, the race was to find GPUs at any price. In 2027, the winners will be the labs that match the duration of their customers’ contracts to the duration of their compute.

---

 Anthropic, PBC Amendment No. 1 to Form S-1 (Form S-1/A), SEC EDGAR CIK 0002130357, Registration No. 333-299633, accession 0001628280-26-068676, filed November 2, 2026 (pp. 138–140, 160, 174–176) : https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026068676/anthropicpbc-sx1ax1.htm . In the third quarter of 2026, Anthropic spent $5.0b on short-term compute alone : 51% of its $9.86b quarterly compute bill : flipping Q2’s $974m GAAP operating profit into a $567m Q3 operating loss even as quarterly revenue grew $5.40b sequentially to $16.96b.  ↩︎   ↩︎   ↩︎

 Per-hour contract rates & confidence bounds combine Anthropic S-1/A contract commitments (pp. 139, 174–176) with public capacity disclosures : SpaceX Form 424B4 final prospectus (filed June 12, 2026, CIK 0001181412, accession 0001628280-26-042639, disclosing $1.25b/month initial fee & ~325,000 NVIDIA GPUs across Colossus 1 & Colossus II : https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1181412/000162828026042639/spaceexplorationtechnologi.htm ; $3.1b/month amended SpaceXAI run-rate across 325,000 GPUs = $13.07/GPU-hour), Anthropic’s May 6, 2026 Colossus 1 announcement (220,000+ NVIDIA GPUs : https://www.anthropic.com/news/higher-limits-spacex ), & the settled October 30, 2026 Ornn B300 Compute Price Index at $12.29/GPU-hour ( https://data.ornn.com/ ).  ↩︎

 Goldman Sachs Commodities Research puts on-time data center delivery over the next one to two years at 50% to 60% (40% to 50% delayed), & JPMorgan (cited by the Wall Street Journal, June 2026) finds that more than 60% of data center capacity planned for 2027 is not yet under construction & a further 7% is delayed ; see Tomasz Tunguz, The Gap Between a Price & a Revenue , October 21, 2026.  ↩︎

 Business Insider, October 20, 2026 : under AWS’s “Early Rack Receipt” program, Amazon took delivery of roughly $5b of Nvidia GB300 racks in August 2026 & ~$3b per month thereafter before facilities had the power to activate them ( https://www.businessinsider.com/amazon-nvidia-ai-gpu-data-centers-power-shortages-2026-10 ).  ↩︎

 Tomasz Tunguz, The AI Bullwhip , August 23, 2026 : generator step-up transformers average three-to-five-year lead times & GE Vernova & Siemens Energy have sold out gas turbine production through 2029.  ↩︎

 Tomasz Tunguz, The Most Important Market in AI Is the Middle , September 23, 2026, & How GPU Prices Can Double While AI Gets Cheaper , September 28, 2026.  ↩︎

 OpenAI Help Center (updated November 2, 2026) & Paul Sawers, OpenAI’s new shared usage limit pits ChatGPT against Codex , The New Stack, November 2, 2026 : starting in December 2026, ChatGPT & Codex on Plus, Pro, & Business plans will draw from a single shared token allowance.  ↩︎

 What’s next
 Over the past year, the size and demands on our monorepo have increased at a staggering pace. It was clear that we needed to revamp our source control system to scale to the level of concurrent work that Codex makes possible.

 We built Pando, a new backend for Git repositories, without interrupting any engineering work or changing how our team uses Git. Pando now powers all development in OpenAI’s monorepo. Pando is designed to meet two ambitious goals: first, horizontally scalable writes, optimized for concurrent pushes to many branches. And second, maximize read throughput, so clients can download data fast enough to fully saturate their available network bandwidth.

 We met these goals while retaining compatibility with the Git protocol and client, enabling both our engineers and agents to seamlessly adopt Pando into their existing workflows. In production, Pando cut median push latency by nearly 5x. It now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day.

 Here, we’ll cover our motivations for building a new source-control system, along with why we chose to retain compatibility with Git. We’ll compare our system with common approaches to scaling Git, describing why Pando is uniquely capable of meeting OpenAI’s scalability needs. We also discuss what’s next, and how we’ll continue contributing to Git to support agent-scale work.

 Why we needed a new source control system

 Codex has changed the scale and pace of development at OpenAI, enabling engineers to do far more work in parallel. That means more branches and pushes, more merges, and more fetches and clones from development environments, research jobs, and CI.

 These demands compound. One engineer now has several changes ready for CI at once, and each push can set several jobs fetching the same commit.

 Starting around the end of last year, the systems supporting our monorepo were struggling to keep up. We suffered slow fetches and pushes along with failed merges, with reliability at times falling below 90%. Had we reached a limit of Git itself, or of the way we served our monorepo? Git grew out of a community that exchanged patches to the kernel via email. For more than two decades, developers have adapted their tools around Git as the way they build software has changed. When we started to feel friction in our own monorepo, it mattered to us that we could keep building on that work.

 We saw a way to keep that familiar workflow while rebuilding the backend to handle pushes to different branches in parallel and serve the same history to many readers concurrently. Building on Git as the foundation of our source-control workflow meant that improvements to the client could be useful beyond OpenAI. We wanted to contribute those improvements from our copy of Git ⁠ (opens in a new window) to upstream, sharing them with the broader community.

 Engineering for Git at scale

 Scaling a source control system has two essential dimensions: many writers pushing to different branches, and many readers fetching the same history. Pando optimizes for both.

 First, Pando coordinates updates to each branch independently. Updates to unrelated branches can proceed in parallel, and a reader fetching a branch gets the history needed for that revision. The tradeoff is that a reader looking at several branches can see them at different points of time.

 Second, Pando reuses packfiles (Git’s format for compressing multiple objects together) across fetches instead of generating an individual packfile for each client. A client may download some objects it already has, but the server can serve the same bytes to many clients with little computation.

 These choices let us scale writes across branches and serve reads from caches. To see how they fit together, let’s start with how Git stores and transfers history.

 Git object storage primer

 Git must be able to keep two parts of a repository in sync: objects and references .

 A Git repository records snapshots of files and the history connecting them as a graph of objects. An object may be either a blob, tree, commit, or tag. Blobs hold the content of an individual file, and trees associate names with blobs or other trees to form a directory structure. Commits point to a root tree and zero or more parent commits, forming the history of your repository.

 Objects are identified by a hash of their type and contents. Objects are also immutable: recording a changed file creates a new blob, while unchanged files and directories can reuse existing objects.

 Branches and tags are references, or “refs”, that point to commits. Committing on a branch creates a new commit and updates the branch’s ref to point to it.

 Git objects reference each other by their ID, commits to trees, and trees to trees and blobs. The branch refs/heads/main points to commit C2, whose parent is C1. C1 points to root tree T1, where parser.py refers to blob B1. C2 points to root tree T2, where parser.py refers to blob B2. In both root trees, docs/ refers to the same tree, T3. Its README.md entry points to blob B3, and usage.md points to blob B4.

 Git stores objects in either a “loose” or “packed” state. Loose objects are stored in individual files identified by their object ID. Packed objects are stored together in a packfile, enabling similar objects to be stored as deltas against one another.

 Git can store blobs as separate files or pack them together, encoding one blob as a delta against another.

 In Git, an object is reachable from a commit if Git can find it by following links from that commit through its parents, trees, and blobs. During a fetch, the client tells the server which commits it wants and which it already has. The server finds the objects reachable from the wanted commits, excludes those it knows the client already has, and sends the remainder as a packfile in the same format Git uses on disk. A full clone starts without any objects, so it needs all the objects reachable from the history being cloned.

 A push transfers objects in the other direction by asking the server to update one or more refs. The client uses the server’s set of advertised refs to avoid sending objects the server already has. The pack being sent can therefore depend on existing objects: receiving the pack alone is not enough to reconstruct the new history.

 Replicating a Git repository means keeping both objects and references available across multiple servers. Before a replica can serve a reference’s new value, it must be able to supply the objects reachable from that value. The service also needs to coordinate competing reference updates , i.e., pushes that try to move the same branch from the same old tip to different new commits. Systems that impose a single order on all writes to a repository can make pushes to unrelated branches wait on one another.

 Existing distributed Git service patterns

 While designing Pando, we evaluated conventional approaches for scaling source control using Git: one that coordinates ref updates across repository replicas using three-phase commit (3PC, a protocol for coordinating a commit across multiple nodes), and one that orders updates through a shared write-ahead log (WAL, a record of changes written before they’re applied) in blob storage.

 Three-phase commit (3PC)

 In the three-phase commit design we modeled, the Git service keeps a complete copy of the repository on several replicas. When any server receives a push, the incoming packfile is copied and sent to all replicas in parallel. To publish the push, a majority of replicas must accept the ref update. The server managing this is the coordinator, and it requires multiple rounds of communication between the coordinator and each other replica.

 To accept a reference update, each replica locks its copy of the ref and checks that it still points to the commit the client expects. The coordinator then sends a pre-commit message to the replicas that accept. Once a majority acknowledges the pre-commit message, the coordinator tells them to perform the update. Any up-to-date replica can then advertise the new branch tip from its local copy of the repository.

 Keeping complete replicas makes it possible to serve reads locally, and guarantees that clients get a consistent view of all references no matter which replica they pick. As a consequence, references are updated one at a time, and each push requires multiple round trips to coordinate the ref update among replicas.

 Waiting for a quorum puts replica disk performance and communication latency on the push path. As write volume grows, the replicas must keep up with incoming packs as well as read traffic.

 Write-ahead log (WAL)

 In the WAL-based design we modeled, the Git service uses a shared manifest in blob storage to order updates across the repository. When a server receives a push, it uploads the incoming packfile to a blob store and prepares the ref update in its local copy of the repository. To publish the push, it adds an entry to a shared manifest stored in the blob store that records the ref update and points to the packfile. The Git server then updates the manifest using a compare-and-swap operation. This atomically replaces the manifest, or otherwise rejects the change. If another writer has updated it in the meantime, the server reads the intervening entries, checks that its ref update is still valid, and retries using the packfile it already uploaded.

 Writers can upload their packfiles in parallel, but even pushes to unrelated branches require updating the same manifest. The round-trip time for a successful compare-and-swap limits how often the repository can publish a new manifest. A low-latency blob store makes this step fast. Batching lets one manifest update several refs at the same time, at the cost of queueing updates and increasing latency.

 The blob store can receive packfiles in parallel, but updates to the shared manifest still compete with one another. Increasing the blob store’s capacity alone doesn’t resolve that bottleneck. Each replica still needs to read and index packs from the blob store before it can serve them locally. If incoming writes outpace that work, replicas fall behind and clients wait longer to fetch newly pushed commits.

 Architecting Pando

 That brings us to Pando. Pando is a new architecture for serving Git repositories with the goal of scaling to many clients pushing simultaneously. Here’s how it works:

 Rethinking constraints

 Prior to developing Pando, we had a hunch that we could meet our requirements without compromising on Git, but we did need to compromise on some of the things that most Git systems assume to be requirements:

 Repository-wide consistency : Providing a consistent, point-in-time snapshot of all refs requires coordination across the repository. In a system that orders all ref updates together, pushes to unrelated branches contend on a single coordination point.

blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: Apple's earnings suggest that the company's hardware business is doing better than ever, even in the face of memory challenges. Does the software story help or hurt?
blogs.content:
Apple's earnings suggest that the company's hardware business is doing better than ever, even in the face of memory challenges. Does the software story help or hurt?

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

Over on Asianometry , Jon explains The Rise of GLM and China’s Zhipu AI , and also gives a trip report from Silicon Valley .

On to the Update:

Apple Earnings

From the Wall Street Journal :

The Apple growth and profit machine is wavering, and the boost from price increases might not be enough to keep it going at historic rates. That dials up the pressure on Apple’s new chief executive, John Ternus. The company saved the bad news for its earnings call, an hour after it posted its results for the September quarter, projecting that for the current quarter its high-margin services business will continue to slow and that its widely watched gross profit margin will continue to fall.

Apple shares had been flat in post-close trading but declined as much as 4% after the company made the projections, which fell short of Wall Street estimates. The impact of high memory costs are weighing even more heavily on the company, Ternus and Apple Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh said on the company’s earnings call. Apple has stockpiled cheaper components purchased earlier, but those inventories are dwindling…

Investors have bid up Apple shares because it has been a port in the AI storm—a reliable and capital-efficient business that stands apart from rivals which are spending hundreds of billions of dollars racing to the AI frontier. While others invest in data centers, Apple has been pouring its own cash into buybacks and dividends. But that safety may be challenged if Ternus can’t speed up Apple’s innovation engine.

Actually, I thought that on his maiden earnings call Ternus made a good case that Apple’s innovation engine is running pretty well:

This is an amazing time at Apple. We just completed one of the most prolific launch periods in our history. It’s been a remarkable time for innovation across all of our categories. One of the greatest testaments to that is the all-new iPhone Duo, the most transformational iPhone since the original. We’re also incredibly excited about iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, which take massive leaps forward on camera, battery life, and performance—features that our users care deeply about. Meanwhile, touch has arrived on Mac for the first time with the all-new MacBook Pro. And we were excited to announce the new iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro. The all-new iPad mini features a stunning new OLED display and brings a super thin design to the smallest member of the iPad family. Apple Watch now offers users the clearest window yet into their heart health. We introduced AirPods 5, which feature industry-leading active noise cancellation in an open-ear design. And we’ve laid the foundation for an even more intelligent smart home with the all-new HomeView, Apple TV 4K, and HomePod mini.

That’s a lot of new products, and the headliner — the iPhone Duo — appears to be a big hit, murmurs about hinge issues notwithstanding. Speaking anecdotally, the response to the device amongst normal users is extremely positive, even if it doesn’t appeal to more hardcore users ; to the extent that is true, that’s a positive sign, in two regards: first, it’s a pleasant reminder that people who obsess over this stuff don’t always represent normal users, and second, there is still room for Apple to segment the market, not just by price but also through fundamental design (as for me, I’m waiting for the Air 2).

Meanwhile, the new MacBook Pro with touch is exactly the computer I’ve been hoping for ever since I first used computers with touch displays at Microsoft 15 years ago. What Microsoft got wrong with Windows 8 was that they overhauled the interface to be touch-first; yes, you can use a mouse-and-keyboard with a touch interface easily enough, but it’s too easy: you give up a lot of power and control in exchange for denominating the user interface by the least precise input method.

Apple didn’t do that: touch is just an extra interaction layer that is there when you need it, and not catered to when you don’t; that’s exactly where Microsoft ended up too, which is why nearly all high-end Windows devices still have touch, even if the operating system long ago reverted towards being built around precise mouse-and-keyboard interfaces. This isn’t a touch-screen computer; it’s a computer that you can touch when and if you find it convenient (and having used them, it’s very nice to have!).

---

Presented by

I spend a lot of time trying to figure out what is happening to businesses on the internet. Luckily, our new advertising partner Stripe has the unique position of processing the equivalent of 1.7% of global GDP, making it, in a sense, a barometer of the economy.

Their latest SaaS data , for example, shows that while SaaS stocks were supposedly experiencing an apocalypse, revenue growth was actually accelerating. You can read about that disconnect on their Stripe Economics blog on Substack.

I suspect there’s a lot more hiding in Stripe’s data and I’m looking forward to having an excuse to dig into it.

---

Memory Problems

Apple first started pushing the narrative that they were a services company in 2016, but, as I argued at the time , that was more aspirational and narrative selling than reality, given the fact the stock market was still focused on iPhone sales; three years later, however, when Apple stopped reporting unit sales and started talking about its installed base I called the switch: Apple was a services company . Three years after that, I was shocked when the company didn’t raise prices in the face of inflation , but I shouldn’t have been: effectively lowering prices — which helps gain market share — is exactly the right approach to take if growing services is the top priority. Indeed, Apple continued to not (or barely) raise prices for years after that, and then came the memory crisis.

It was memory that dominated the Q&A on the earnings call, and it’s hitting Apple on multiple fronts. First, even with June’s price increases (which didn’t include the iPhone), margins were down by about one percentage point because of memory. Second, even with price increases both in September (on the iPhone) and October (on Macs and iPads, above and beyond the summer’s increase), margins will decrease by another 1.5–2 percentage points. Moreover, Ternus said it’s going to get worse:

Let me give you an overall view on memory. What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented, and as we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carry-in inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components. Now, for the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs, partly offset by a few factors. So, as we said, we changed the price on many of our products, including Mac and iPad at the end of June, and iPhone in September, and these price increases provided some offset. We also expect to see some benefit from carry-in inventory in the December quarter as well, as well as lower costs on certain non-memory components. And looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase. As we said before, we do believe we will see a decreasing benefit from the carry-in inventory on memory over time. And there is one more thing I wanted to add. As we work to improve supply, our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by $33 billion from June to the September quarter, which you’ll see in our annual filing when it comes out tomorrow. Now back to Kevan for the other parts of it.

That last bit is point number three: Apple is having to make significant purchase obligations to secure memory, likely locking in these high prices. Fourth, despite those purchase obligations — or perhaps because purchase obligations are necessary — Apple actually doesn’t have enough memory! This was COO Sabih Khan, the second new addition to the earnings call:

So during the September quarter, we experienced supply constraints on iPhone, Mac and iPad, and this was driven by the high levels of demand, and as we’ve said before, we’re seeing less flexibility in the supply chain than normal. The Q4 constraints were primarily driven by the availability of the advanced nodes our SOCs are produced on, but as we have transitioned more of our lineup to the latest 2nm technology nodes, our constraints on advanced nodes are easing. And for the December quarter, we expect constraints on Mac and iPad, primarily driven by memory, as demand has been higher than what we expected.

I made this point previously in the context of those SoC constraints, which is that Apple isn’t just used to dictating price to suppliers, but also having the freedom to ramp its manufacturing up and down in response to demand while forcing those suppliers to maintain the capacity and inventory to meet their needs. Now, however, Apple has to actually forecast demand, knowing that if they forecast too low they won’t sell as much as they could have, and if they forecast too high they are the ones who have to carry excess inventory.

The Hardware Company Regression

The good news for Apple goes back to the innovation question: the company is consistently missing its forecasts by underestimating demand. Of course it would be ideal if the company had enough devices to sell to everyone who wanted one, as soon as they want it, but in the grand scheme of things it’s good news that Apple devices seem to be more popular than ever. Moreover, that popularity is increasing even as the price increases. CFO Kevan Parekh was, understandably, unwilling to say this was a trend:

If I kind of unpack the comments around supply chain, about availability of components, and your outlook for the December quarter, can you help us understand sort of the difference or maybe the delta of quantity versus price across the product lineup? Because it certainly looks like you’re looking at double digit growth across the iPhone and the Mac business, and we all know, I think, in the industry that there’s been pretty strong price inflation across the PC/Mac ecosystem, and you guys mentioned that you’ve reluctantly taken price as well. So can you help us understand kind of what’s the driving dynamics in that market?

KP : We don’t normally provide that level of detail or color as we look at the outlook, other than to say, again, we did guide to the 7% to 10% year on year, and again, just as a reminder, that is on top of a phenomenal December quarter last year, where revenue grew 16%, and so we don’t provide the level of detail, but I would say it’s early to really read price elasticity at this point in time. The iPad and Mac were constrained since we had made those adjustments, and again, we just recently just adjusted the price on iPhone, so it’s really early to really assess any elasticity impact at this stage.

This explains why I was so shocked when Apple didn’t raise prices four years ago; from the very beginning of Stratechery I’ve been wondering just how high Apple could raise prices without significantly hurting demand, and well, the seeming answer — just as it was with the iPhone 5S vs 5C, and just as it was with the iPhone X — is significantly higher!

There is, however, one fly in the ointment; this was the paragraph that came after Ternus’ opening extolling Apple’s hardware launches:

On top of it all, we’re unlocking more powerful AI experiences across our lineup, including with the all-new Siri AI, a profoundly capable and deeply personal assistant seamlessly integrated across our platforms. And like everything we make, Siri AI is built with essential privacy protections so no one can access users’ data, not even Apple. We launched Siri AI in beta for US English users in Septem...
